Third article: whether the more universal things are prior in our intellectual cognition.

Regarding the third point, it proceeds thus. It seems that the more universal things are not prior in our intellectual cognition, because those things which are prior and better known by nature are posterior and less known to us. But universals are prior by nature because that from which the consequence of existing does not convert is prior; therefore, universals are posterior in the cognition of our intellect. Furthermore, composite things are prior in relation to us than simple ones. But universals are simpler; therefore, they are later known in relation to us. Furthermore, the philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the first book of the *Physics* that the defined falls into our cognition before the parts of the definition. But the more universal things are parts of the definition of the less universal; for instance, animal is a part of the definition of man; therefore, universals are later known in relation to us. Furthermore, we arrive at causes and principles through effects. But universals are certain principles; therefore, universals are later known in relation to us. But against this is what is said in the first book of the *Physics*: that from universals it is necessary to arrive at singulars. I answer that it must be said that in the cognition of our intellect, two things must be considered. First, that intellectual cognition in some way takes its beginning from sensitive cognition. And because sense is of singulars, while the intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the cognition of singulars be prior in relation to us than the cognition of universals. Second, it must be considered that our intellect proceeds from potency to act. Now, everything that proceeds from potency to act arrives at the incomplete act, which is intermediate between potency and act, before it arrives at the perfect act. The perfect act to which the intellect arrives is complete science, through which things are known distinctly and determinately; but the incomplete act is imperfect science, through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For what is known in this way is known in a qualified sense in act, and in a way in potency. Hence the philosopher says in the first book of the *Physics* that those things that are first manifest and certain to us are more confused; later, however, we know by distinguishing the principles and elements. It is manifest, however, that to know something in which many things are contained without having proper knowledge of each one of those things contained within it is to know something under a certain confusion. Yet in this way, both the universal whole in which the parts are contained in potency and the integral whole can be known; for either whole can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being known distinctly. However, to know distinctly that which is contained in the universal whole is to have knowledge of a less common thing; just as to know animal indistinctly is to know animal insofar as it is animal. But to know animal distinctly is to know animal insofar as it is rational or irrational, which is to know man or lion. Therefore, it occurs to our intellect to know animal before it knows man. And the same reasoning holds if we compare any more universal thing to a less universal thing. And because sense departs from potency into act just as the intellect does, the same order of <column-break/>cognition appears in the sense. For we judge the more common before the less common according to the sense, and according to both place and time. According to place, indeed, as when something is seen from a distance: it is first grasped as being a body before it is grasped as being an animal, and it is first grasped as being an animal before it is grasped as being a man, and first a man before Socrates or Plato. According to time, because a child from the beginning distinguishes man from non-man before he distinguishes this man from another man. And for this reason, children at the beginning call all men fathers. Later, however, they determine each one, as is said in the first book of the *Physics*. And the reason for this is manifest: because he who knows something indistinctly is still in potency to know the principle of distinction, just as he who knows the genus is in potency to know the difference. And thus it is clear that indistinct cognition is intermediate between potency and act. Therefore, it must be said that the cognition of singulars is prior in relation to us than the cognition of universals, just as sensitive cognition is prior to intellectual cognition. But both according to the sense and according to the intellect, the cognition of the more common is prior to the cognition of the less common. To the first, therefore, it must be said that the universal can be considered in two ways. In one way, according to the fact that the universal nature is considered simultaneously with the intention of universality. And since the intention of universality—namely, that one and the same thing has a relation to many—proceeds from the abstraction of the intellect, it is necessary that in this way the universal be posterior. Hence, in the first book *On the Soul*, it is said that the universal animal is either nothing or is posterior. But according to Plato, who posited subsistent universals, according to this consideration, the universal would be prior because particulars, according to him, are nothing but by participation in the subsistent universals which are called ideas. In another way, it can be considered regarding the nature itself, namely of animality or humanity as it is found in particulars. And thus it must be said that there is a twofold order of nature. One is according to the path of generation and time, according to which path those things which are imperfect and in potency are prior. And in this way, the more common is prior according to nature, which appears manifestly in the generation of man and animal. For animal is generated before man, as is said in the book *On the Generation of Animals*. The other is the order of perfection or the intention of nature, just as act is simply prior according to nature than potency, and the perfect is prior to the imperfect; and in this way, the less common is prior according to nature than the more common, such as man than animal. For the intention of nature does not stop at the generation of the animal, but intends to generate man. To the second, it must be said that the more common universal is compared to the less common as a whole and as a part: as a whole, indeed, according to which not only the less universal is contained in potency in the more universal, but also others; as under animal, not only man but also horse is contained. As a part, however, according to which the less common contains in its definition not only the more common but also others, as man [contains] not only animal but also rational. Thus, therefore, animal considered in itself is prior in our cognition than man. But man is prior in our cognition than [the fact] that animal is a part of his reason. To the third, it must be said that some part can be known in two ways. In one way, absolutely, according to what it is in itself; and thus nothing prevents one from knowing the parts before the whole, such as stones before a house. In another way, according to the fact that they are parts of this whole; and thus it is necessary that we know the whole before the parts. For we know a house by a certain confused cognition before we distinguish its individual parts. Thus, therefore, it must be said that those things which define are to be considered absolutely as known before the defined; otherwise, the defined would not be made known through them.
